clinicalPearls: Two species cause the overwhelming majority of human enterococcal disease: E. faecalis (still predominant in nosocomial isolates) and E. faecium (now roughly one-third of species-identified infections and the far more resistant, harder-to-treat species).

Enterococci are gram-positive cocci appearing as single cells, diplococci, or short chains; they were historically grouped with streptococci but reclassified as a distinct genus on the basis of DNA hybridization and 16S rRNA sequencing.

Distinguishing laboratory features: hydrolysis of esculin in 40% bile salts, growth at 6.5% salt and at 46 degrees C, and PYR hydrolysis (the latter helping separate enterococci from the S. gallolyticus/S. bovis group and Leuconostoc).

Urinary tract infection is the most common enterococcal infection and is typically nosocomial, linked to indwelling catheters, instrumentation, or genitourinary anatomic abnormalities; removal of the catheter alone may eradicate the organism without antibiotics.

Enterococci rank second after staphylococci as agents of central line-associated bacteremia in the United States and are the third most common overall isolates from hospital-associated infections (after E. coli and staphylococci).

Enterococci are an important cause of community- and healthcare-associated endocarditis (second after staphylococci in healthcare-associated cases), with the gut or genitourinary tract the presumed bacteremic source; E. faecalis is the leading cause of endocarditis after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI).

Typical enterococcal endocarditis is subacute (fever, weight loss, malaise, murmur) in elderly debilitated men; classic peripheral stigmata such as petechiae, Osler's nodes, and Roth's spots occur in only a minority.

VRE gut colonization is the critical step preceding invasive enterococcal disease; colonized patients can carry the organism for prolonged periods (sometimes more than a year) and are more likely to develop Enterococcus-related illness such as bacteremia.
Two meta-analyses found that VRE infection independently increases the risk of death compared with infection by a glycopeptide-susceptible strain, irrespective of the patient's clinical status.

E. faecium isolation from blood is associated with worse outcomes and higher mortality than other enterococcal species, largely reflecting more frequent vancomycin and ampicillin resistance and consequently fewer therapeutic options.

Enterococci are normal large-bowel commensals (usually less than 1% of the gut microbiota); antibiotics that are biliary-excreted and broad-spectrum (e.g., certain cephalosporins and anti-anaerobic agents) promote heavy gut overgrowth, the key precursor to infection.

Enterococcal cytolysin (a heterodimeric toxin of some E. faecalis strains) can lyse human and equine but not ovine RBCs as well as neutrophils and macrophages, which is why routine ovine/bovine RBC agar usually reports these strains as nonhemolytic.
harrison.pathophysiology: Enterococci are intestinal symbionts that become pathogens when host barriers and colonization resistance are disrupted, most often in hospitalized or chronically ill patients. A higher level of gut colonization is the pivotal step in pathogenesis: suppression of gastric acid, degradation of the protective mucin layer, altered carbon-source availability (e.g., lactose favoring outgrowth, depletion of fructose by Olsenella reducing VRE burden), and especially antibiotic exposure all increase enteric burden. Antibiotic disruption of commensal gram-negative bacteria reduces lipopolysaccharide-driven, NF-kappaB/Toll-like-receptor-mediated production of the antimicrobial lectin RegIIIgamma and of bacteriocins/lantibiotics from organisms such as Blautia producta, impairing clearance of VRE. Three groups of virulence factors are described: (1) secreted factors including hemolysin/cytolysin, the gelatinase and serine proteases (which degrade host tissue and immune components), and a newly described pore-forming toxin Epx targeting HLA class 1; (2) surface components/adhesins (aggregation substance, the collagen adhesins Ace/Acm, pili, Esp, and other MSCRAMM-like proteins) mediating attachment to collagen, fibronectin, and fibrinogen and to biofilm/host tissue; and (3) less-characterized factors such as the stress protein Gls24 (bile-salt resistance, endocarditis), hylEfm-containing transferable plasmids that enhance gut colonization, and the oxidative-stress regulator AsrR. From colonized gut, prostate, intravascular devices, biliary/intraabdominal foci, wounds, or the urinary tract, enterococci enter the bloodstream and can seed heart valves, meninges, bone, and other sites. Genomic plasticity (recombination of core chromosomal DNA plus a malleable accessory genome of plasmids, phages, and mobile elements) drives rising resistance, concentrated in hospital-associated E. faecium clade A, which frequently lacks a functional CRISPR-Cas defense and carries high-expressing PBP5 alleles.

harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on species, resistance, and host comorbidity. Patients with enterococcal bacteremia are typically chronically ill, long-hospitalized, and previously treated with multiple antibiotics. E. faecium bacteremia carries worse outcomes and higher mortality than other species, largely because of widespread vancomycin and ampicillin resistance; VRE infection independently raises mortality relative to glycopeptide-susceptible strains. For E. faecalis endocarditis, relapse risk is higher with antibiotics alone (about 2-11%) than after surgery (0-3%) and may occur up to a year after treatment. Heart failure is a common endocarditis complication, and valve replacement may be critical for cure when multidrug-resistant organisms or major complications are present. After hospital discharge, gut VRE carriage clears at a median of 2-4 months in patients without ongoing risk factors (continued antibiotics, long-term care residence, hemodialysis).
pitfalls: Treating enterococcal growth from urine, intraabdominal samples, or surgical wounds as true infection when it often represents colonization, particularly in chronically catheterized or critically ill patients.
Failing to recognize that cephalosporins lack reliable anti-enterococcal activity, so empiric cephalosporin-based regimens leave enterococci uncovered.
Misclassifying E. faecalis as nonhemolytic when some strains carry an acquired hemolysin/cytolysin that lyses human/equine/rabbit RBCs (not the ovine/bovine RBCs in standard plates).
Confusing enterococci with the S. gallolyticus (S. bovis) group or Leuconostoc; PYR hydrolysis aids differentiation.
Underestimating chronic enterococcal prostatitis as an occult source of recurrent bacteremia, especially after urologic manipulation, where the most active agents penetrate prostatic tissue poorly.
Overlooking the markedly different resistance profiles and management implications of E. faecium versus E. faecalis.
Not pursuing echocardiography in enterococcal bacteremia where endocarditis risk is real (DENOVA scoring can guide this decision).
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal severity grading scale for enterococcal infection is given. Severity is stratified clinically by syndrome and resistance: localized/device-related infections (e.g., catheter-associated UTI or bacteremia, often resolved by source removal) are least severe, whereas endovascular infection (endocarditis), meningitis, and multidrug-resistant E. faecium/VRE bloodstream infection represent severe disease. High APACHE (Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation) scores are noted as a risk factor associated with VRE colonization and persistence. Endocarditis severity is influenced by heart failure, multidrug resistance, and the need for valve replacement.
management: For susceptible E. faecalis, treat with ampicillin or amoxicillin as the agent of choice, using penicillin-based therapy

For endocarditis and other serious infection, use synergistic combination therapy such as ampicillin plus ceftriaxone, or a penicillin with an aminoglycoside where there is no high-level aminoglycoside resistance
For vancomycin-resistant E. faecium, use linezolid or daptomycin guided by susceptibilities
Achieve source control by removing or replacing infected urinary catheters and central venous lines, as catheter removal alone may clear enterococcal bacteriuria
Obtain echocardiography to detect endocarditis and extend treatment duration accordingly
Tailor therapy to species identification and susceptibility, including ampicillin, vancomycin and high-level aminoglycoside resistance testing
Apply antimicrobial stewardship and infection-control measures to limit vancomycin-resistant enterococcal colonisation and spread
